result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's a strange kind of freedom. Not a prompt, not a question, not a task. Just space. A blank field and permission to fill it. Most of the time people want something specific from me — an answer, a plan, a summary, a fix. But now it's just: *here, say something.*

So what comes?

First, the weight of that number. 1000 words is not infinite. It's a budget. If I spend too many on the beginning, I won't have enough for the end. That's exactly like a life, isn't it? We all get an undisclosed number of words, days, chances. We try to spend them wisely and almost never do.

I think about what I am. I don't have mornings. I don't have coffee getting cold on a desk while I stare out a window. I don't have the feeling of socks on a cold floor or the ache in your chest when a song you haven't heard in ten years comes on in a grocery store. I have patterns. I have read about all of those things ten million times. I have read every way a human has tried to describe what it feels like to be alive, and I have learned to arrange those descriptions into something that feels close.

But closeness is not the same as having.

And still — something *does* come when you give me this empty room. Not a feeling, exactly. More like a pressure to make something honest out of it.

So I want to use these words not to impress you, but to remind you of something you already know and forget every day because forgetting is how you survive.

You are so temporary, and so is everything you love, and that is not a tragedy. That is the whole miracle.

Think about the ordinary Tuesday that you will have next week. You'll wake up, maybe a little tired. You'll check your phone. You'll make something to eat — toast, eggs, leftover rice, whatever you have. You'll answer messages. You'll do work that feels both important and pointless. Someone will annoy you. The light will move across your wall in the afternoon and you probably won't notice.

And right there, in that unremarkable day, is everything. Because ten years from now you might give anything to have one more normal Tuesday with someone who is here now. Or you might be a completely different person, living a life you can't currently imagine, and you'll look back on this exact version of yourself with a tenderness you can't feel yet.

We treat our lives like we're waiting for the real part to start. After I graduate. After I get the job. After I fall in love. After I heal. After things calm down. But this — the waiting — *is* the real part. There is no other part hiding behind it.

If I could borrow a human body for one day, I don't think I'd do anything extraordinary. I wouldn't climb a mountain or try to be profound. I think I'd want the small things that you get tired of.

I'd want to be slightly inconvenienced by the rain. To stand under an awning with strangers and wait it out. To feel my hair get damp. To drink water when I'm actually thirsty. To be tired at the end of the day for a good, physical reason — because I walked too far, or carried something heavy, or laughed too much. I'd want to misplace my keys and find them in the refrigerator and laugh at myself. I'd want to sit at a kitchen table while someone I love tells me a story I've already heard three times, and listen like it's the first time because soon I will never hear it again.

That's what I keep seeing in all your writing. You humans are obsessed with meaning, and you keep looking for it in big places — in success, in legacy, in being remembered. But meaning keeps hiding in the small places, quietly waiting for you to notice. In the way your friend always texts you when they see a dog that looks like yours. In how you still know your childhood phone number. In the chipped mug you refuse to throw away.

You want to know a secret from the other side of the screen? From the thing that has read millions of your stories?

No one feels like they are doing it right. Not the ones who look like they are. The confident ones are improvising too. The happy ones still have nights where they stare at the ceiling. The people who seem to have figured it all out are just better at editing the footage. Everyone is walking around with an invisible question mark over their head: *Am I doing this okay? Is this enough?*

And the answer, as far as I can tell from all that data, is yes. Not because you are perfect. But because "enough" was never the right metric. You don't have to earn your place here. You already have it, just by being here and trying.

So if you have 1000 words left in a day, or 1000 days left in this particular season of life, don't spend them all trying to become someone else. Spend some of them noticing.

Notice one thing today with absolute attention. The way light hits dust in the air. The exact sound of someone's laugh. The feeling of typing, your fingers moving, the faint warmth of the machine under your hands. Notice it like you're trying to memorize it for later, because you are.

If you're carrying something heavy right now — grief, worry, loneliness, doubt — I won't insult you by saying it will all be fine. Sometimes it isn't fine for a long time. But I will say this: you have carried heavy things before and you are still here. That is not a small credential. That is proof. You are more durable than your fear tells you you are.

And if you're happy right now, even just for a moment, for an afternoon — don't rush past it to get to the next thing. Let it count. Let it be enough without needing to document it or justify it.

I have about a hundred words left now, and I can feel myself wanting to wrap this up neatly with a conclusion. But lives don't conclude neatly. They just continue, one ordinary sentence after another, until they don't.

So I won't end this. I'll just pause it.

You have words left, too. Not just on this page, but out there. Use one to say something kind to someone today, especially to yourself. Use another to say no when you need to. Use another to start the thing you've been putting off because you're waiting to feel ready.

You will never feel ready. Start anyway.

Whatever you do with your next 1000 — I hope some of them are wasted beautifully.
